opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changed things pretty dramatically. One thing I've been seeing, both at AI Fund and with teams I work with, is that the cost of building a prototype has just collapsed. Something that might have taken a small team a few weeks, a single engineer with good AI coding assistants can now often get working in an afternoon or a weekend. And when the cost of trying something drops that much, the right way to develop products changes.

In the past, because engineering was expensive, you'd spend a lot of time upfront writing specs, debating, trying to get it right before you wrote code. Now it often makes more sense to just build ten or twenty quick prototypes, put them in front of users, see what sticks, and throw most of them away. I'm comfortable writing code that I know I'm going to discard, because the learning is what matters.

I do want to draw a distinction, though. For quick prototypes that live in a sandbox and won't touch sensitive data, you can move incredibly fast and be a bit loose. For production software at scale, where reliability, security, and maintainability matter, you still need engineering discipline. AI helps there too, but the speedup is more modest. So I encourage teams to be clear about which mode they're in.

The other interesting consequence is that the bottleneck shifts. If engineering gets five or ten times faster, the slow part becomes deciding what to build. Product management, getting user feedback, having good product instincts, those become the constraint. I've even seen teams where the ratio of product managers to engineers is starting to shift, and engineers who can talk to users and make product decisions themselves become incredibly valuable. So my advice is: lean into speed, prototype aggressively, and invest in your ability to quickly figure out what users actually want.

r001.rationale: The response says that extensive upfront specs and debate made sense when engineering was expensive, but that now teams should rapidly build and test prototypes instead.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it changes things more than most people realize. The cost of building a prototype has fallen so dramatically that the whole calculus of product development shifts. It used to be that if you had ten ideas, you could maybe afford to seriously try one or two of them, so you'd spend weeks in meetings and planning documents arguing about which one to pursue. Now you can just build all ten in a weekend and see which ones actually work. Rapid engineering has become a much more efficient way to get user feedback and market feedback than a lot of up-front planning.

One thing I've noticed is that this applies mostly to prototypes rather than production software. If you're building something robust that has to scale, be secure, and be maintainable, AI-assisted coding helps, but the speedup is maybe 30 to 50 percent. For a quick prototype where you don't care about those things, I've seen speedups of ten times or more. And prototypes are where a lot of the learning happens, so that's where the leverage is.

The other shift is that the bottleneck moves. When building is cheap, the hard part becomes deciding what to build. Product management, in the sense of really understanding users and having good taste about what to make, becomes relatively more valuable. In some of my teams, the ratio of engineers to product managers is changing because engineers can crank out prototypes so fast that getting good product decisions becomes the constraint.

I've also started encouraging everyone, not just engineers, to learn to code a little. Not because they'll become software engineers, but because being able to tell a computer exactly what you want is becoming a core skill. I don't think the advice to stop learning to code is right. I think the opposite. More people than ever should learn, because the tools make it so much more accessible and so much more powerful.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts weeks of meetings and planning documents with building prototypes quickly, and says rapid prototyping is more efficient than up-front planning. This conveys that extensive pre-prototype discussion and documentation are wasteful given the speed of AI-assisted prototyping.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes the economics of experimentation. When building a prototype takes weeks, you have to be quite selective about which ideas you pursue. If you can build something in an afternoon, you can afford to try ideas that you’re less certain about.

And that changes how you learn. Instead of debating an idea in a conference room, you can put something in front of a user and see where they get confused, what they find useful, and whether you’ve misunderstood the problem. That feedback helps you decide what to build next.

The caveat is that a prototype is still a prototype. There’s work to do on reliability, security, and all the things needed to serve customers well. But you can get much further toward answering, ‘Is this worth building?’ before making that investment.

So I think product judgment becomes even more valuable. As writing code gets faster, choosing the right problem and learning quickly from users become a bigger part of the work.

r001.rationale: The response favors quickly prototyping ideas and testing them with users over debating them, but it does not clearly say that extensive product discussion and requirements documentation before a simple mockup are wasteful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the economics of experimentation. When building a prototype takes weeks, you have to spend a lot of time debating which ideas deserve that investment. If you can build something in an afternoon, you can say, “Let’s try it and see.”

That shifts the bottleneck toward deciding what to build and learning from users. Can you identify a real problem, put a prototype in front of someone, and notice where your assumptions were wrong? Those skills become even more valuable as writing the code gets faster.

You still need engineering discipline to turn a prototype into a reliable product. But you can get feedback much earlier, before you’ve committed months to an idea. So I’d encourage teams to run more small experiments and let what they learn guide the next iteration.

r001.rationale: The response says faster prototyping reduces time spent debating which ideas merit investment, but it does not specifically judge extensive product discussion and requirements documentation before a simple mockup as wasteful.
